title: EARLY Act Reauthorization of 2025
official_title: To reauthorize the Young Women's Breast Health Education and Awareness Requires Learning Young Act of 2009.
likelihoodReason: Introduced by Rep. Debbie Wasserman Schultz (D-FL-25) with 20 cosponsors and a cross-party original cosponsor group including Reps. Miller-Meeks (R-IA), Fitzpatrick (R-PA), Harshbarger (R-TN), Castor (D-FL), and Dingell (D-MI). The House-passed measure was referred to the Committee on Energy and Commerce and now moves to the Senate. Short reauthorizations of expiring CDC public-health authorizations that shift the year window without changing dollars are the profile that typically clears the Senate by unanimous consent or voice.

referencedSources.label: 42 U.S.C. 280m (Section 399NN of the Public Health Service Act — EARLY Act)

summary: The Young Women's Breast Health Education and Awareness Requires Learning Young Act of 2009 (Section 399NN of the Public Health Service Act, 42 U.S.C. 280m) directs CDC to run a national evidence-based public education campaign and a health-care-professional education campaign on breast health, symptoms, early detection, and support for young women (defined as women 15 to 44) diagnosed with breast cancer; the Act also funds prevention research and grants to organizations serving young women with breast cancer. This bill extends the program's authorization of appropriations by striking the current "2026" end year in subsection (h) and inserting "2031", extending $9M-per-year authorization through fiscal year 2031.
brief: Extends the CDC-run EARLY Act young women's breast health and support program's $9M-per-year authorization through fiscal year 2031.

top_lines.headline: What the EARLY Act Does
subs: CDC national public education campaign on breast health and early detection
Health-care-professional education campaign on symptoms, family history, referrals
Prevention research on breast cancer in younger women
Grants to organizations providing information and support to young women diagnosed with breast cancer
"Young women" defined as women 15 to 44 years of age

top_lines.headline: What This Bill Changes
subs: Extends the $9M-per-year authorization from FY2022-2026 through FY2031
No changes to the underlying program activities or eligibility

sections.label: Section 2 — Reauthorization of the Young Women's Breast Health Education and Awareness Requires Learning Young Act of 2009

items.main: Extends the EARLY Act authorization of appropriations by striking "2026" and inserting "2031" in Section 399NN(h) of the Public Health Service Act (42 U.S.C. 280m(h)).
items.detail: The referenced statute currently authorizes $9M for each of fiscal years 2022 through 2026 to carry out subsections (a) (public education campaign), (b) (health-care-professional education), (c)(1) (CDC prevention research), and (d) (support for young women diagnosed with breast cancer). This bill's one operative amendment shifts the end year of that authorization from 2026 to 2031 without changing the dollar figure or the scope of the covered activities.

gaps: The bill extends the authorization through FY2031 but does not adjust the $9M-per-year dollar figure — the amount has been held flat since the 2020 amendment (Public Law 116-260) and is not indexed for inflation.

The bill continues the "young women" statutory definition of women 15 to 44 but does not address whether the CDC campaign and research should specifically account for higher-risk populations flagged in the underlying statute (Ashkenazi Jewish populations, racial and ethnic minority groups).
The bill does not modify the Advisory Committee established under Section 399NN(a)(4) — including its membership or its reporting obligations to Congress.
The bill continues the every-3-year impact measurement requirement under Section 399NN(f) but does not require CDC to make its measurement data publicly available.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Fitzpatrick
featured_quotes.text: I am proud to co-lead this critical legislation, Mr. Speaker, to reauthorize the Breast Cancer Education and Awareness Requires Learning Young, or EARLY Act, a proven lifesaving initiative that promotes early detection and education for young and high-risk women. Breast cancer remains the most common cancer among women, with over 300,000 new cases and 42,000 projected deaths in 2025. I have seen the power of early detection up close, Mr. Speaker. Both my mom and my sister are breast cancer survivors. This is a very, very personal issue.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Guthrie
featured_quotes.text: I commend my colleague. I know he talked about his mom and his sister, but as we all know, those of us who have been here a little bit of time, his brother was our colleague and had cancer as well. We miss him. May God bless his family.

featured_quotes.name: Ms. Wasserman Schultz
featured_quotes.text: To my colleague from Pennsylvania (Mr. Fitzpatrick), I was proud to be elected in the same class as his late brother, Mike. He was a good and decent man, someone who always reached across the aisle. I was really fortunate to be able to serve with him and with the current Congressman Fitzpatrick. First, I thank Chairman Guthrie and Ranking Member Pallone for their strong support of this legislation, because one in eight American women, as you have heard, will get breast cancer, and 42,000 are expected to lose their life from it this year.

modified: Section 399NN(h) of the Public Health Service Act (42 U.S.C. 280m(h)) — authorization end year shifted from "2026" to "2031", extending the $9M-per-year authorization through FY2031
